clue.text: Pasta recipe? Voila! Introduction to Italian cooking

parts.note: R is the recipe abbreviation, the one that heads a prescription
five of the six letters that go into the pan
the introduction to ITALIAN supplies the sixth

explanation.walkthrough: R for recipe is a chemist's convention crosswords borrowed long ago. Note where this puzzle is set: nearly every surface from here on is a kitchen, and the food words are usually the fodder rather than the meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasta → RAVIOLI: definition by example — one named kind of stuffed pasta, so the general word fairly covers the particular one.

clue.text: Reasonable portion: a large

parts.note: a ration is a measured portion of food
the letter lifted straight out of the clue
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.walkthrough: The colon does the misdirection: it makes 'Reasonable portion' read as one phrase, when the definition stops after the very first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Reasonable → RATIONAL: both mean guided by reason rather than feeling, though RATIONAL leans clinical where 'reasonable' leans polite.

clue.text: In half-dark toilet after very hot curry

parts.note: V is the standard abbreviation for very
the word taken as it stands
the first half of DARK
LOO is the everyday British toilet, and a crossword workhorse

explanation.walkthrough: V for very and LOO for toilet are two abbreviations worth banking. The queasy joke the surface is making about a vindaloo and a lavatory is doing all the misdirection.
explanation.definitionFit: hot curry → VINDALOO: a Goan dish that British curry houses have made shorthand for the fiercest heat on the menu.

clue.text: After the start, adore new kitchen appliance

indicators.note: after the start means everything following the opening letter, so the first letter of the word for adore is dropped

parts.note: to adore is to love

explanation.surface: Once you get going, you will adore your new cooker.
explanation.walkthrough: 'After the start' keeps what follows the first letter of LOVE, leaving OVE.
explanation.definitionFit: An oven is the enclosed heated compartment of a cooker in which food is baked or roasted.

clue.text: Egg feeding two in Rome completely unknown as a starter

parts.note: II is the Roman numeral two, and it splits to take a filling
a nit is a louse's egg
ALL does duty for completely, as in 'all done'
algebra's unknown quantities are X, Y and Z

explanation.walkthrough: The egg here is the louse's, not the hen's — NIT is the crossword staple, and 'feeding' is a swallowing instruction rather than a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: as a starter → INITIALLY: both are adverbial and mean at the outset; the food theme is daring you to read 'starter' as a first course.

clue.text: Something good for you, varied in taste, taking beginners one minute

parts.note: the beginners of Varied In Taste
'a' is one, as in a minute meaning one minute
MIN is the everyday abbreviation for minute

explanation.walkthrough: Three initials and then two abbreviations: the answer is made entirely of shorthand, which is exactly why the surface can stay so smooth.
explanation.definitionFit: Something good for you → VITAMIN: a functional definition, not a synonym — vitamins are named precisely by the fact that a diet needs them.

clue.text: Utter failing to eat nothing

parts.note: a vice is a moral failing
O is the round nothing, zero

explanation.walkthrough: 'Utter' is the verb, not the adjective — you utter and you voice an opinion. Eating as an instruction to swallow one piece inside another is worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: Utter → VOICE: both are verbs for saying something aloud, though VOICE leans towards making a view public rather than simply speaking.

clue.text: Blending hot tripe with icing in the end? This creates a problem with balance

definitions.text: This creates a problem with balance

parts.note: eight of the nine letters, waiting to be blended
the end of ICING supplies the ninth

explanation.walkthrough: The definition works by consequence rather than description: a tightrope is not itself a problem with balance, it is the thing that sets one.
explanation.definitionFit: This creates a problem with balance → TIGHTROPE: defined by what it does to you, a rope stretched taut being the classic test of poise.

clue.text: In a stew, brief period before microwave's indication that it's finished

parts.note: a mo is a moment — old slang crosswords keep alive
the ping a microwave sounds when its timer runs out

explanation.walkthrough: The long second fragment is a description rather than a synonym: there is no abbreviation to spot, just the noise the machine makes.
explanation.definitionFit: In a stew → MOPING: both describe someone sunk in low, fretful spirits instead of getting on with things; the theme wants you to picture a casserole.

clue.text: Something in fish for example I can cut up at home

indicators.note: cut up means chopped into pieces, so these letters are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
in means at home, as in 'staying in'

explanation.surface: A cook offers to chop up something fishy in their own kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cut up' rearranges I CAN into NIAC before IN. The definition is a description: fish is one food that contains the vitamin.
explanation.definitionFit: Niacin is vitamin B3, found in foods such as fish, meat and whole grains.

clue.text: Assemble ingredients making chewing easier

indicators.note: the anagram indicator, disguised as a recipe instruction

parts.note: eleven letters, exactly the enumeration

explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue reads as a line from a cookbook, which is the trap: 'Assemble' is telling you to rearrange letters, not to cook anything.
explanation.definitionFit: making chewing easier → TENDERISING: the process word for softening meat by beating or marinating, so the food gives the teeth less work.

clue.text: Chop the end off fruit and vegetable

indicators.note: chopping the end off a word removes its last letter

parts.note: a pear is a fruit

explanation.surface: A recipe instruction to trim the end of a fruit and a vegetable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chop the end off' removes the final R of PEAR.
explanation.definitionFit: A pea is the small round green seed of a pod, eaten as a vegetable.

clue.text: Flavour comes back somewhat similar to an egg

parts.note: f-LAVO-ur holds the letters, and an across entry coming back reads them right to left

explanation.walkthrough: Reversed hidden words are the hardest to spot, because the letters look wrong until you read the other way. 'Somewhat' is the tell that only part of a word is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: similar to an egg → OVAL: the adjective for an egg's exact outline, and the word descends from Latin ovum, an egg.

clue.text: Enthusiasts of diet sandwiches left thank-you note before tea delivered

parts.note: the word that gets sliced open after its second letter
L is the standard abbreviation for left, and it is the filling
TA is the informal thank-you
N abbreviates note
the sol-fa note TI is written differently but said exactly like 'tea'

explanation.walkthrough: The answer keeps its Italian plural: one dilettante, several dilettanti. 'Delivered' is the sound instruction — a speech is delivered aloud.
explanation.definitionFit: Enthusiasts → DILETTANTI: amateurs who dabble in an art for love of it, so the definition catches the enthusiasm and politely drops the dabbling.

clue.text: Sherry in the morning acceptable before a party

parts.note: ante meridiem, the hours before noon
the British idiom — something unacceptable is 'just not on'
till and before both mean up to a point in time
the letter lifted straight out of the clue
a do is a party, another crossword regular

explanation.walkthrough: Five pieces, none longer than four letters, and every one of them an everyday word — the difficulty is entirely in seeing where to cut.
explanation.definitionFit: Sherry → AMONTILLADO: definition by example, a medium-dry style from Jerez standing in for the drink as a whole.

clue.text: Deals with type of unhealthy fat, then gets down to business

parts.note: trans fats are the notoriously unhealthy kind
to act is to stop deliberating and do something

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are ordinary English doing double duty: 'trans' is only half a word until the fat names it, and 'acts' is buried in a business idiom.
explanation.definitionFit: Deals with → TRANSACTS: both are verbs for conducting business with someone, TRANSACTS being the formal, contractual register of the pair.

clue.text: Lacking a clear plan, prepare ham or soup

indicators.note: the anagram indicator, reading as kitchen work

parts.note: nine letters of lunch, exactly the enumeration

explanation.walkthrough: AMORPHOUS literally means without shape, from the Greek morphe. Watch how 'or' sits inside the fodder and looks like a choice you are being offered.
explanation.definitionFit: Lacking a clear plan → AMORPHOUS: the figurative sense of shapeless, used of vague and unstructured things rather than of physical form.

clue.text: Supplier's broth is nutritional at the core

parts.note: stock is the broth a soup is built on
the word taken as it stands
the middle letter of the eleven in NUTRITIONAL

explanation.walkthrough: That 's is only joinery, not a possessive to unpick — spotting it is half the battle. The pleasure is STOCK doing duty as both broth and shop inventory.
explanation.definitionFit: Supplier → STOCKIST: retail jargon for a shop authorised to carry a maker's goods, so it supplies at one remove rather than manufacturing.

clue.text: Secretly plan hot, dependable stuffing with essence of figs

parts.note: hot in the fashionable sense is IN
dependable is TRUE, and it is about to be stuffed
the essence — the middle — of fIGs

explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' meaning fashionable is the step to find, and the comma sitting after it is doing its best to make you read heat instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Secretly plan → INTRIGUE: the verb sense, to scheme covertly, which survives mainly in writing while the noun does the everyday work.

clue.text: May unfortunately see can contains rejected mushroom starch component

indicators.note: unfortunately suggests things going wrong, so the letters of May come out in the wrong order
contains means holds inside, so the reversed mushroom sits within the pair of words for see and can

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning see or behold
a tin is a can

indicators.note: rejected means turned back, so the word for mushroom is read backwards

parts.note: a cep is an edible mushroom, the porcini

explanation.surface: Someone called May finds that a can of mushrooms has gone off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'unfortunately' rearranges MAY as AMY; 'rejected' turns CEP into PEC, and 'contains' puts it between LO and TIN.
explanation.definitionFit: Amylopectin is one of the two polysaccharides, with amylose, that make up starch.

clue.text: Sweet made sharper with addition of iodine

parts.note: to hone a blade is to make it sharper
I is iodine's chemical symbol

explanation.walkthrough: HONIED is the older spelling of honeyed and perfectly sound; the crossing letters are what tell you which of the two the setter wants.
explanation.definitionFit: Sweet → HONIED: sweetened with or as if with honey, and by extension the adjective for flattering, over-sugared talk.

clue.text: Course is enough for one doing the work of five

parts.note: if a thing serves, it is enough for the purpose
the Roman numeral five, whose job I takes over
the Roman numeral one, which moves in

explanation.walkthrough: The clue describes a job swap and means a letter swap: Roman numerals let 'one doing the work of five' be read as I standing in for V.
explanation.definitionFit: Course → SERIES: a course of lectures or of antibiotics is precisely a series of them, the sense that survives in that phrase.

clue.text: Finished small pastries at last after flipping flake fails to rise

indicators.note: after places the final piece following the reversed word

parts.note: over means finished, as in 'the game is over'
S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels

indicators.note: flipping means turning over, so the word for flake is read backwards

parts.note: to peel is to flake off, as paint does

indicators.note: at last means the final letter of the word

parts.note: its last letter is S

explanation.surface: A baker's small pastries have flopped: the flaky dough refuses to rise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fails to rise' looks like a baking failure, but it means not getting up on time. 'flipping' turns PEEL into LEEP, and 'after' puts the S from 'pastries at last' behind it.
explanation.definitionFit: To oversleep is to sleep too long and so not get up at the intended time.

clue.text: Burned when initially forgotten, as cereal typically is

indicators.note: initially forgotten means the first letter is left out

parts.note: seared means burned or scorched on the surface

explanation.surface: Toast gets burned when you forget it, as breakfast cereal often does.
explanation.walkthrough: 'when initially forgotten' drops the S from SEARED. Cereal here is the crop in the field, not the breakfast food.
explanation.definitionFit: Cereal plants such as wheat and corn bear their grain in ears, so they are described as eared.

clue.text: Spoil escargot partway through

parts.note: hidden in the middle of the French word for snail, running straight through without a break

explanation.walkthrough: One word long enough to bury a four-letter answer is all a hidden clue needs, and an unusual menu item is always a good place to start looking.
explanation.definitionFit: Spoil → SCAR: both are verbs for damaging a surface for good, SCAR carrying the sense of a mark left behind rather than outright ruin.

clue.text: Bread on American menus from Pisa — feta not reliable

parts.note: run PISA and FETA together, then strike out the letters S, A, F and E; what's left, read in order, is the answer
reliable is SAFE, the four letters that 'not' removes

explanation.walkthrough: Nothing is shuffled here: strike the letters of SAFE out of the town and the cheese and the answer survives in its original order.
explanation.definitionFit: Bread on American menus → PITA: the American spelling of the flatbread Britain writes as PITTA, so the geography is doing real defining work.

clue.text: Chemical company at one time dissolving biscuit in odd locations

parts.note: B, S, U and T sit in the odd positions of BISCUIT and dissolve away

explanation.walkthrough: Alternate-letter clues are usually flagged by 'odd' or 'even'; here 'odd locations' names the letters that GO, not the ones that stay.
explanation.definitionFit: Chemical company at one time → ICI: Imperial Chemical Industries, a British giant broken up and finally swallowed by AkzoNobel, hence the past tense.

clue.text: Char occasionally good, as the French say, in emerging "extreme grilling"

parts.note: the alternate letters of C-h-A-r
something emerging is rising
BON is French for good, and it drops in behind the R

explanation.walkthrough: 'Char' looks like the definition and is really the fodder — the setter has put the cooking word exactly where you expect the meaning to be.
explanation.definitionFit: extreme grilling → CARBONISING: burning food to carbon is grilling taken past all usefulness, and the quotation marks admit the definition is a joke.

clue.text: Deli on the fringes marinated missing duck left to rot

parts.note: the fringes of DELI, its outer letters
marinated is SOUSED, with the duck's O gone missing
a duck is a zero in cricket, hence the letter O

explanation.walkthrough: Duck for O comes from cricket's scoreboard and is one of the most useful conventions there is. SOUSED means both pickled and drunk, which the surface enjoys.
explanation.definitionFit: left to rot → DISUSED: not quite a synonym — DISUSED says only that nothing uses the thing any more, and the decay is what follows.

clue.text: Surprise! After brief wait trifle, if dropped, reconstituted

indicators.note: brief means cut short, so the last letter of the word for wait is lost

parts.note: to stay is to wait or remain

indicators.note: reconstituted means made up again in a new form, so the remaining letters are rearranged
dropped means left out, so the letters of if are taken from the dessert's name

parts.note: taken as written: a layered British dessert of sponge, custard and cream
taken as written

explanation.surface: After a short wait, a dropped trifle is put back together, to everyone's surprise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'brief' cuts STAY to STA; 'if dropped' takes I and F from TRIFLE, leaving TRLE, which 'reconstituted' rearranges as RTLE.
explanation.definitionFit: To startle someone is to give them a sudden shock or fright, which is what surprising them does.
